name: The Great Gatsby
blurb: F. Scott Fitzgerald's Jazz Age novel of a mysterious millionaire and his lost love
title: The Great Gatsby Summary: Plot, Characters and Ending Explained
description: The Great Gatsby summary: who Nick, Gatsby, Daisy and Tom are, what happens chapter by chapter, the ending explained and what the green light means.
h1: The Great Gatsby: Summary, Characters and Ending Explained
answer: The Great Gatsby is a 1925 novel by the American writer F. Scott Fitzgerald, set on Long Island and in New York City in the summer of 1922. It is narrated by Nick Carraway, a young bond salesman from the Midwest who rents a small house next to the mansion of Jay Gatsby, a rich and secretive man famous for his parties. The novel follows Gatsby's attempt to win back Daisy Buchanan, a woman he loved years earlier, and looks at wealth, class and the American Dream in the Jazz Age.

head: Character
Who they are
rows: The narrator, a Yale graduate and World War I veteran working in the bond business
Nick's neighbor in West Egg, a young millionaire whose past is the subject of rumors
Nick's cousin, a charming woman from a wealthy family, living in East Egg
Daisy's husband, a rich, arrogant former college football star
Daisy's friend, a professional golfer who becomes involved with Nick
Tom's mistress, who longs to escape her marriage
Myrtle's husband, who runs a garage in the valley of ashes
Gatsby's business associate, a gambler with underworld connections

body: Chapters 1 to 3: In spring 1922 Nick moves to West Egg, the Long Island village of new money. Across the bay in East Egg, home of old money, he dines with Daisy and Tom and meets Jordan Baker, who tells him Tom has a mistress in New York. That night Nick sees Gatsby alone on his lawn, reaching toward a green light across the water. Tom later takes Nick to the valley of ashes, a grim dumping ground between Long Island and the city, where a faded billboard of the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg looks down on George Wilson's garage. Tom collects Myrtle and they party at an apartment in Manhattan until Tom breaks Myrtle's nose for repeating Daisy's name. Nick is then invited to one of Gatsby's huge parties, where guests trade wild stories about their host, and he meets Gatsby without at first realizing who he is.

Chapters 4 to 6: Gatsby takes Nick to lunch with Meyer Wolfsheim, who is said to have fixed the 1919 World Series. Jordan explains that Gatsby and Daisy fell in love in Louisville in 1917, when he was a young officer with no money; while he was overseas she married Tom. Gatsby bought his mansion to be across the bay from her and threw his parties hoping she might come. At Gatsby's request Nick invites Daisy to tea, and the two are reunited; Gatsby shows her his house and his collection of shirts, and they begin an affair. Nick learns that Gatsby was born James Gatz to poor farmers in North Dakota and remade himself at seventeen, learning the habits of wealth from a millionaire, Dan Cody. Daisy and Tom attend a party, and Daisy dislikes it. Gatsby wants more than an affair: he wants Daisy to tell Tom she never loved him, so they can return to the past.

Chapters 7 and 8: On a hot day the group drives into the city and takes a suite at the Plaza Hotel. Tom confronts Gatsby, reveals that his fortune comes from bootlegging and other criminal deals, and Daisy, pressed to say she never loved Tom, cannot. Tom sends her home with Gatsby in Gatsby's yellow car. On the road through the valley of ashes, Myrtle, who has been locked in by George after he discovered her affair, runs into the road and is struck and killed. Daisy was driving, but Gatsby intends to take the blame. Gatsby keeps watch outside the Buchanans' house that night while Tom and Daisy sit together at their kitchen table. The next day George, convinced the driver was Myrtle's lover, learns from Tom that the car belongs to Gatsby. George finds Gatsby floating in his pool, shoots him dead, and then kills himself.

Chapter 9: Nick tries to arrange a funeral. Daisy and Tom have left town without a forwarding address, Wolfsheim refuses to come, and almost none of the party guests attend; Gatsby's father, Henry Gatz, arrives from Minnesota proud of his son. Nick ends things with Jordan, meets Tom on Fifth Avenue and learns that Tom told George where to find Gatsby, and decides to go home to the Midwest.

On his last night in West Egg, Nick walks to Gatsby's empty house and looks across the bay, thinking of the green light at the end of Daisy's dock and of the Dutch sailors who first saw the green island of the New World. He reflects that Gatsby believed in a future that kept slipping away, and that all people keep pushing toward it. The book ends with a famous line: "So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past."

The literal outcome is bleak: the careless rich survive unharmed, while Myrtle, George and Gatsby are dead. Nick describes Tom and Daisy as careless people who smashed things and let others clean up after them. Readers usually take the ending in a few overlapping ways:

ul: A verdict on the American Dream: Gatsby's self-made wealth cannot buy entry into old-money society or recover the past, and the dream itself is shown as hollow or corrupted by money.
A story about the impossibility of repeating the past: Gatsby's real goal is not Daisy as she is but the moment in 1917, which no effort can bring back.
A portrait of Nick himself: he calls himself honest, but he also helped the affair along, so some readers treat him as a partly unreliable narrator whose admiration for Gatsby colors the story.

body: These readings are standard in criticism and classrooms; none of them comes from a single statement by Fitzgerald.

ul: The American Dream: Gatsby's rise from James Gatz to millionaire is both inspiring and empty.
Old money and new money: East Egg's inherited wealth looks down on West Egg, and Tom uses class to defeat Gatsby.
The past: Gatsby believes the past can be repeated, and the whole plot tests that belief.
Carelessness and moral decay: the parties, the affair and the hit-and-run show a society without responsibility.
Symbols: the green light stands for Gatsby's hope, and the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg watch over the valley of ashes like an absent god.
Length: nine chapters, a short novel of under 200 pages in most editions.
Adaptations: films in 1926, 1949, 1974 (directed by Jack Clayton) and 2013 (directed by Baz Luhrmann), plus TV films, an opera and stage musicals.
Content advisory: domestic violence, a fatal car accident, a murder and a suicide.
What teachers usually ask about: the green light and other symbols, Nick as narrator, East Egg versus West Egg, and whether Gatsby deserves to be called great.

check.q: Who is driving Gatsby's car when it kills Myrtle Wilson?
check.why: Daisy was at the wheel, and Gatsby planned to take the blame for her.
George Wilson, told by Tom that the car was Gatsby's, shoots him in his pool and then kills himself.
Gatsby was born James Gatz to poor farmers and changed his name as a teenager.

faq.q: What does the green light mean in The Great Gatsby?
faq.a: The green light at the end of Daisy's dock is Gatsby's hope of winning her back and, more broadly, the dream of a future always just out of reach.

faq.q: Where does Gatsby's money come from?
faq.a: Tom reveals that Gatsby made his fortune through bootlegging and other illegal deals linked to Meyer Wolfsheim; Gatsby's stories about inherited wealth are false.

faq.q: Does Daisy go to Gatsby's funeral?
faq.a: No. Daisy and Tom leave town without a forwarding address, and almost no one attends apart from Nick and Gatsby's father.
